title: Why deep water looks blue
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: Why is a glass of water clear but the ocean blue?

explain.say: A glass of water looks clear, but a deep lake or sea looks blue. That is because water itself is very slightly blue, and you only notice it when there is a lot of water.
Water molecules absorb red light a little. In a glass that hardly matters, but within about five metres of sea water most red light is gone.
Deeper down, orange and then yellow light are absorbed too, while blue light travels farthest. So the deeper the water, the bluer the light that is left.
Light that dives into the sea and scatters back up to your eye has lost its red on the way, so the water looks blue. A clear blue sky reflecting off the surface adds even more blue.

faq.a: Water absorbs red, orange and yellow light more than blue. Sunlight that goes into deep water and scatters back has lost those colours, so it looks blue. Reflected blue sky adds to it.
asks: Is the sea blue because of the sky?

faq.q: Is a glass of water blue too?
faq.a: Very slightly, but the effect is so weak that you need metres of water to notice. That is why a glass looks clear but a deep pool or the sea looks blue.
asks: Why is water clear in a glass?

faq.a: Water soaks up the warm colours first: red within a few metres, then orange and yellow. Divers find that a red swimsuit looks dull brown or grey at depth.
asks: Why does red look grey underwater?

faq.q: Why is some sea water green or brown?
faq.a: Tiny floating algae, mud or dissolved matter change the colour. Algae make coastal water look green, and river mud can make it brown.
asks: Why is the sea sometimes green?
Why is the water murky near the shore?

faq.q: Why is the sea grey on a cloudy day?
faq.a: On cloudy days there is no blue sky to reflect and less sunlight going in, so the sea reflects grey clouds and looks dull grey.
asks: Why does the sea change colour?
Is the sea blue when it is cloudy?

facts: Pure water absorbs red light slightly, giving thick layers of water a pale blue colour.
Underwater, red light is mostly lost within the first few metres, while blue light penetrates deepest.

quiz.say: A diver's red flipper looks dull brown at 20 metres deep. Why?
quiz.show: Red looks dull deep underwater because…

options.show: The water has absorbed the red light above
options.say: The water has absorbed the red light above

quiz.why: Red light is absorbed in the first few metres of water, so there is little red left to reflect off the flipper.

wrong.1: The dye is unchanged; bring it up and it is red again.
wrong.2: Pressure does not change colour; it is the missing red light.
